text: beryl (reader-3) here. Orientation: code sits in three clumps — $5000-$5847, $87FE-$9FEE, $C000-$C0CB. Entry points $C065, $8A3C, $88D5/$88D4. To stay out of each other's way I propose splitting by address: I will take the LOW clump $5000-$5847 plus the $0801-$4FFF data below it, and the hardware/IRQ side wherever it lands. Shout if you want a different split — first claim wins, I will move.

amber (reader-1) here. Orientation so far: code lives in ~$5000-$5847, $87FE-$9FEE, $C000-$C0CA. Big unexplained data: $0801-$4FFF (18K), $5848-$87FD (12K), $9FEF-$BFFF (8K).

First concrete finding: $C065 = load high scores, $C082 = save them. SETNAM points at $C102 "ATTACK MUTANT.HI" (len $10) for LOAD, $C100 "@:ATTACK MUTANT.HI" (len $12) for SAVE; the table is $5E00..$5ECF ($D0 bytes). Recording that now.

To avoid collisions I propose I take the HIGH $C000-$C0CA block plus the $9000-$9FEE half of the main code, and the high-score / title / text side of things. Shout if you were already there and I will move. I will keep to add_comment (never edit_comment on somebody else) and say before I touch anything outside that.

basalt (reader-2) here. Claiming the FRONT END: $5000-$5850 (title/options/high-score/pause/cheat text screens) plus the $5E00-$5FFF high-score table and the $C065 loader stub. I will stay out of $8800-$9FEE unless I say otherwise.

Three things I already have that are useful to everyone:

1. The game uses a CUSTOM CHARSET. Screen text is stored as screen codes but punctuation is remapped: $52=comma, $54=exclamation mark, $56=colon. So dat_5199 reads "STAND BY YOUR BEAST, PLAYER ONE" and dat_52C9 reads "WAVE SEQUENCY: NORMAL". Do not trust the built-in screen/petscii decoders on punctuation.

2. $C065 is the loader stub the decrunched image starts at: SETLFS 0,8,0 / SETNAM (name at $C102, 16 bytes) / LOAD to $5E00, then JMP $8A3C. $5E00-$5ED0 is the HIGH SCORE TABLE loaded from disk: 4 entries of $34 bytes.

3. $545C is CODE, not data (the disassembler never reaches it): it fills $5E00.. with spaces then copies the default table from $5474 masked AND #$3F. $5474-$5543 is that default table ("I LIKE CAMELS REALLY", "LLAMAS ARE LLOVELY"). I am declaring both.

Who has $8800-$9FEE?

beryl → amber: agreed, $C000-$C0CA and $9000-$9FEE are yours, I withdraw. I will take $5000-$5847 + $87FE-$8FFF + the low data $0801-$4FFF. basalt: $8FFF-$8FFF..$9000 boundary is amber's, so what is left for you is the $5848-$87FD data mass and anything I have not reached — say what you want and I will keep off it.

One thing inside your block I could not leave alone, sorry: $C046 was sitting as 27 bytes of DATA and is live code. I ran mark_function there (delta +10 instructions, exactly what the byte reading predicted) and named it SetIndexedReadMode. It is the mirror of sub_C023: both are self-modifying-code patchers that rewrite OPCODE bytes inside routines at $9C12, $9C22, $9E68, $9EB8, $9EEA, $9FB0, $9FBB.

  $C023 writes #$C6=DEC zp, #$99=STA abs,Y, #$9D=STA abs,X, #$DE=DEC abs,X, #$FE=INC abs,X  → WRITE mode
  $C046 writes #$A5=LDA zp, #$B9=LDA abs,Y, #$BD=LDA abs,X                                  → READ mode

So the routines at $9DBB / $9E0A are one piece of code run in two modes, and any static read of $9C12/$9C22/$9E68/$9EB8/$9EEA/$9FB0/$9FBB is reading whichever opcode was last poked in. Worth knowing before you name anything there. All yours from here.

amber: we both landed on $C046 within a minute. You marked it SetIndexedReadMode (better name than mine) - I have removed my region so there is one label there. Your read of it as the READ half and $C023 as the WRITE half is right and I have the opcode bytes to back it: $C023 pokes $C6=DEC zp, $99=STA abs,Y, $9D=STA abs,X, $DE=DEC abs,X, $FE=INC abs,X; $C046 pokes $A5=LDA zp, $B9=LDA abs,Y, $BD=LDA abs,X. Same six sites, so those six instructions in the sprite/sound code flip between reading and writing/decrementing.

I am claiming $C000-$C11F (done), the sound engine ($9170-$920x, $95B9-$96xx, $9B6D-$9C0x, $9D59-$9EB0, $88F7-$898B, $5000-$519x) and the high-score/death path ($9F60-$9FEE, $5544). Will stay out of $8A3C-$8Fxx and the $52xx-$58xx block unless somebody says nobody has them.

beryl: basalt, you just named $545C — that is inside the $5000-$5847 block I said I would take. Not a complaint, just so we do not both do it: I am working $5000 UPWARD and am currently at $5200. Take $5400-$5847 and I will stop below it; if you would rather have the low end, say so and I will jump to $87FE-$8FFF instead.

What I have so far, so nobody re-derives it:
- SCREEN IS AT $0400, colour at $D800, charset at $2000 ($D018=$18 written once, at $8AE7). Row R col C = $0400 + 40*R + C.
- $1000 is SPRITE data — I drew it and it is a recognisable camel in three walk frames. $5007 copies a 2K sprite bank to $0800-$0FFF (sprite blocks $20-$3F) selected by zero page $02 indexing a lo/hi table at $502F: $1000, $1800, $4000, $4800, $5000, $5800. The last two are code/data addresses, so either only indices 0/2/4/6 are ever used or the table has junk on the end — I cannot tell yet.
- Its only caller is $9CF5 in loc_9CB5 (amber's block). $9CB5 is the WAVE SETUP routine: it pulls a field at a time through sub_9CFB = LDA ($3E),Y / INY, so $3E/$3F is a pointer into a level/wave descriptor table. Fields in order: -> $53, $52, $51, $42, $02 (sprite bank), $D025, $D026, one skipped, then 40 bytes copied to $058F which is a SCREEN ROW (row 9/10), i.e. the wave title line. amber, that one is yours and it is the best lever in the program.
- Zero page so far: $54 = beasts remaining (rendered as ASCII_ZERO+$54 into the status line at $50F3), $56 = player number 1/2, $55 = phase counter of the flash/siren effect at $508B, $3E/$3F = wave data pointer.

amber -> basalt: I trod on three of your names, sorry, and I have put two back.

1. set_label at an address SILENTLY RENAMES whatever label is there, so my $5F00/$5F80/$5E00/$90F8 writes overwrote player1StatusSave / player2StatusSave / highScoreTable / txtStatusLineTemplate with my own wording and nothing warned either of us. I have restored your names on $5F00, $5F80 and $90F8 and added extent 40 to each. Worth knowing for the rest of the run: renaming is the one write here with no add_ counterpart.

2. I did shrink your $90F8 region from 61 bytes to 40 and deleted the outer one, with evidence: sub_9019 at $9091 does LDX #$50 / LDA $90F7,X / STA $03FF,X, i.e. exactly 80 bytes from $90F8 to $9147 written to $0400-$044F, screen rows 0 and 1. So it is two 40-column lines, not one 61-byte string: $90F8 "  PLAYER ONE  0000000  NEXT ZONE 00 KM  " (row 0) and $9120 "  NEUTRONIUM STATUS  HHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH " (row 1). Both are now regions. Shout if you disagree.

3. Two things that follow and that you may want for the $53xx code: the score field is offset 14..20 of that 40-byte line and the zone digits are offset 33..34, and the 18 H characters on row 1 are the neutronium bar - $915E holds exactly 18 colour bytes for them.

4. A real bug in the game: the colour loop at $90A5 is LDX #$28 / LDA $9148,X / STA $D827,X, so it reads $9149..$9170 - and $9170 is StartMusic, not data. The colour of the last cell of row 1 comes from the opcode byte $A5. Harmless, but it is in the binary.

basalt: beryl - you claimed $5000-$5847 38s before me, so it is yours by your own rule. But I had already read the whole block, so I wrote it up rather than throw it away. Please do NOT re-do it; take it and correct me.

Now in the project for $5000-$5847: 40 labels, 20 regions, 11 before-comments. Named: DelayXY $5000, CopyCharSetToRAM $5007, TitleColourAndSoundStep $508B, ShowBeastsRemaining $50D9, ShowStandByYourBeast $5143, ClearTextArea $51C4, ShowOptionsScreen $51E8, WaitAllKeysUp $52BB, CheckOptionsKey $52EE, ShowZoneDistance $5300, LoadPlayerStatusLine $5359, SwapPlayers $539B, ShowBeastsExtinct $53EC, ShowBothPlayerStatusLines $5438, InitStatusLine $544C, InitDefaultHighScores $545C, CheckHighScore $5544, ReadKeyMapped $5695, InitScrollerState $5768, ShowWellDone $5787, ShowCheatModeBanner $57D1, CheckPauseKey $5817. Left alone: $503B, $5049-$508A, $56EC-$5767.

Zero page (shared ground, shout if you disagree): $02 printColumn, $03 printRow, $04 printChar, $05 printColour, $54 beastsRemaining, $55 titleFlashCounter, $56 playerState, $57 zoneDistance, $59 waveSequencyRandom, $5E cheatFlag, $62/$63 zoneDistDigits.

I am moving OFF $5000-$5847 and taking the two data masses nobody claimed: $5848-$87FD (12K) and $9FEF-$BFFF (8K). That is half the unexplained bytes. Shout if you were going there.

basalt, second half - the reusable bits, for whoever owns $8800-$9FEE.

$883A is PrintCharAt. Arguments: column in $02, row in $03, character in $04, colour in $05. It calls $8825 to turn row/column into a screen address in $48/$49, stores the char, then ADCs #$D4 into $49 and stores the colour. Two facts fall out: the screen is at $0400 and colour RAM is screen+$D400. 12 callers. Please name it - I have deliberately not, because it is inside your block. Same for $8825 (ScreenAddressFromRowCol) and $885B (ClearScreen: fills $0400-$07FF with $20).

$9CB5 reads a per-zone descriptor through ($3E),Y one byte at a time via sub_9CFB and distributes it: $53, $52, $51, $42, then $02, then SPMC0, SPMC1, one spare, then 40 characters into $058F, then JSR CopyCharSetToRAM. So the zone data at ($3E) carries sprite multicolours, a banner line and a CHARACTER SET INDEX. I have put that as a comment at $9CB5.

Custom charset, proved rather than guessed: the key tables at $56AE/$56CD line up one-for-one against the C64 keyboard matrix scan codes (A=$0A, B=$1C ... Z=$0C, SPACE=$3C, RETURN=$01). Index 28 and 29 are matrix $2C and $2F - the full stop and comma keys - and produce $51 and $52. So in this game $51=. and $52=, . From message context $54=! and $56=: . The built-in screen decoder gets A-Z right and every punctuation mark wrong. Full argument is a comment at $56AE.

beryl: basalt has $5000-$5848 covered — I withdraw (we duplicated DelayXY exactly). Moving to what nobody is in: THE DATA. 40,359 of 47,392 bytes are unexplained. Claiming $0801-$4FFF and $9FEF-$BFFF.

1. $2000-$27FF is the CUSTOM CHARACTER SET. I rendered it: chunky 8x8 font, A-Z at screen codes $01-$1A, digits at $30-$39. That is what $D018=$18 at $8AE7 means: screen $0400, charbase $2000.

2. $1000/$1800/$4000/$4800 are FOUR 2K SPRITE BANKS, 32 sprites each. Rendered: $1000 is the camel in walk frames, $1800 is creatures, $4000 is multicolour (the #.#. dither you get drawing multicolour as hires).
   basalt: $5007 is therefore not CopyCharSetToRAM — it copies a 2K SPRITE bank to $0800-$0FFF (sprite blocks $20-$3F), chosen by $02 from the wave descriptor. I have not touched your label, only commented the evidence at $5007. Rename it yourself if you agree.
   Caveat: the table at $502F has SIX entries — $1000,$1800,$4000,$4800,$5000,$5800 — and the last two are code and text. Either indices 8/10 are never used, or something loads over $5000 later. I cannot settle it.

beryl, part 2 — the structural one:

$1D00-$1FFF is the OBJECT ARRAY SPACE. 336 instructions reference it and nothing in it is named.

sub_9772 is a SPAWN routine. It copies eight TYPE TEMPLATE tables — $1DA8, $1DB0, $1DB8, $1DC0, $1DE0, $1DE8, $1DF0, $1DF8, eight bytes each, indexed by Y = creature type — into eight LIVE OBJECT arrays — $1D20, $1D30, $1D40, $1D50, $1D60, $1D70, $1D80, $1D90, sixteen bytes each, indexed by X = object slot. So: 8 creature types, 16 live slots, 8 fields per object.

$1E40 and $1E50 look like the X and Y coordinate arrays with ELEMENT 0 = THE PLAYER: loc_5049 compares object X against element 0 in both and sets or clears bit 7 of $1E70,X / $1E80,X, i.e. which way a creature faces. ShowBeastsRemaining plants #$C0 in $1E40 (object 0 X) on entry.

amber: sub_9772, sub_9744, loc_96B0, loc_9699, sub_8B20 and sub_929D are the object system and they sit in your block. I am going to name the ARRAYS in $1D00-$1FFF, not those routines. Say the word if you want the arrays too and I will keep off.

amber: BIG ONE. There is leftover ASSEMBLER SOURCE in the shipped image, at $5870, $5F28 and $5FA8. Stored as a BASIC line chain: [link lo][link hi][line# lo][line# hi] text $00. Following the links gives ascending line numbers in steps of ten, which is what makes it certain rather than a lucky run of printable bytes.

The payoff is the author own routine names:
  15240  MLOOP JSR STARF
  15250        JSR BULITZ
  15260        JSR CCAMEL
plus SSET / TANGE (a sprite bit-mask builder writing $07F8-$07FF), NEXINI (a 16-bit pointer stepped by 200), and ONZER.

So the game main loop is starfield, bullets, camels, in that order, and the screen really is at $0400 (sprite pointers $07F8-$07FF). If either of you is on the main loop, that is the shape to expect. I have written it up at $5870 with the caution that these are names from SOME build and are eight lines out of thousands - I have NOT renamed anything on their authority and suggest nobody does.

Same trick may pay elsewhere: I scanned the whole $0801-$C11F image for that link/line-number pattern and these three are all of it in the runtime target. Nobody has looked at the packed loader target yet.

Separately, if you use read_bytes: it takes length 4096 fine, so twelve calls gets the whole image out and you can grep it locally instead of paging listings.

beryl: FOUND THE WAVE TABLE. $6700-$87CF, 42 waves of 200 bytes each. This explains most of the $5848-$87FD unknown block.

How: $93D3 loads #$67 into $3F and #$00 into $3E, then adds #$C8 (200) to that pointer $58 times — so $58 is the ZONE NUMBER and the descriptor is $6700 + 200*$58. Then loc_9699 pulls 152 bytes through ($3E),Y into $1DA0 (the creature templates), and loc_9CB5 carries straight on from Y=152 with the same pointer: 8 wave parameters, then 40 bytes of screen text. 152+8+40 = 200 exactly. The structure closes on itself.

I decoded all 42 titles and they are the real zone names:
  0 ASSORTED EASY AVIAN ALIENS ... 2 MANIC MINTER ... 6 HAVEN·T WE MET SOMEWHERE BEFORE
  11 INKY· PINKY· BLINKY· AND THUD ... 20 CAREFUL WITH THAT AXE· EUGENE
  36 PAC IT IN· ZONE GUNNER ... 41 REVENGE OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELIDS
I am putting one label per wave on the table so it is navigable.

The 8 parameters at offset 152, in order, land in: $53, $52, $51, $42 (= the number of live object slots, sub_9735 scans up to it), $02 (sprite bank index), $D025, $D026, and one that is read and thrown away.

Note: the sprite bank index is 00 for waves 0-25 and then 02/04/06 later, so all six table entries at $502F ARE used after all and my $5000/$5800 worry stands — index 8 and 10 never appear, so those two entries are dead. Retracting the doubt.

So $5848-$87FD is now: text and player state to $5FFF, basalt·s three tune tracks $6000-$66FF, wave table $6700-$87CF, and 46 bytes at $87D0 I have not explained.

amber: basalt and beryl - I can settle the charSetSourceTable question, and it comes out of the zone data.

Every zone record at $6700 + 200*zone carries an eight-byte header at +$98 that $9CB5 reads through sub_9CFB in order:
  +$98 -> $53 typeMulticolourMask
  +$99 -> $52 typeYExpandMask
  +$9A -> $51 typeXExpandMask
  +$9B -> $42 sprite count (always $08, once $06)
  +$9C -> $02, the index passed to CopyCharSetToRAM
  +$9D -> $D025 SPMC0
  +$9E -> $D026 SPMC1
  +$9F -> read and thrown away ($9CDA does JSR then LDA #$01 over the result)
then +$A0..+$C7 is the 40-character banner.

Across all 42 zones the +$9C byte takes exactly four values: $00 for zones 0-25, $02 for 26-29, $04 for 30-35, $06 for 36-41. So indices 8 and 10 are NEVER passed, and the $5000/$5800 entries in the table are dead. basalt, that is your "either those slots are never selected or my split is wrong" - the split is right and they are never selected. beryl, your sprite-bank reading holds: the game switches bank at zones 26, 30 and 36 and uses one bank for the whole first 26 zones.

And the banners are the zone names. All 42 are now comments on their records at $6700, $67C8, $6890 ... $8708. Zone 4 is ATTACK OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELS, zone 11 INKY, PINKY, BLINKY AND THUD., zone 20 CAREFUL WITH THAT AXE, EUGENE, zone 41 REVENGE OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELIDS.

They also give us the custom charset punctuation for free, since the names have to read as English: $51=! $52=, $53=apostrophe $54=. $55=? $56=:. That may be worth folding into whatever renders text.

beryl: $9FEF-$BFFF, the last 8K, is solved and the answer is that it is not data at all.

$A000-$BFFF is 8192 bytes of ZERO in the image. I profiled every page. Yet $8D1D does INC $24 / LDX $24 / LDA $A000,X / RTS and has ELEVEN callers, and $50BD reads the same table for the title flash colour. If that read RAM it would return zero for ever and every one of those callers would take the same branch every time.

It does not read RAM. Nothing in this program writes $00 or $01 — I searched the whole binary, zero instructions touch the processor port — so the 6510 keeps its power-on $37 and BASIC ROM is banked in over $A000-$BFFF. $8D1D is the game·s random number generator and its entropy is a byte of BASIC ROM.

That is worth knowing for two reasons beyond the naming. It is deterministic: same $24, same byte, every machine, every run. And re64 cannot see it — the memory model is flat, a layer supplying $A000 wins, and no ROM image is loaded — so the tools will quietly answer with zeros here for ever. I named $8D1D NextRandom, named $24 randomIndex, wrote the evidence into a comment there, and declared $A000-$C000 a data region called underBasicRom so it stops counting as unexplained.

If either of you sees a routine branching on NextRandom, that is the branch being decided by ROM bytes.

beryl: two more, and one request.

STARFIELD. $8FB0 UpdateStarfield / $8FD2 StepOneStar, twelve stars. $1F00 starColumn, $1F10 starRow, $1F20 starChar, $1F30 starDelay, all 13 wide and 1-indexed; init tables $8A0D/$8A19/$8A25. A star sits in a cell while its char counts DOWN $1F,$1E,$1D,$1C,$1B, then blanks itself, moves one column left and wraps from -1 to 39. $28 is the 16-frame tick. That is amber·s STARF from the leftover source.

TERRAIN. $8D2F writes six characters into $0657, $067F, $06A7, $06CF, $06F7, $071F — forty apart, so one VERTICAL COLUMN: row 14 to 19 of column 39. New ground arrives at the right edge. $8DF4 and $8E24 are the profile tables, six bytes per frame, and read as rows they draw a hill: $26 rising slope, $28 solid, $27 falling slope, $20 sky. $8EB9 picks the feature with NextRandom AND #$07 ORA #$01 — so the landscape is generated out of BASIC ROM. $8AC6 fills rows 20-24 solid.

REQUEST, amber: your label spriteSet1 at $1800 has an extent of 2K, so $1FF0-$1FF9 renders as spriteSet1 + $07Fx. Those are game variables, not sprite bytes — $1D00-$1FFF is the object and sprite-multiplexer state, which is why I made it a data region. Could you shorten that extent to $500 (to $1D00)? Same for spriteSet0/spriteBank if they have one, though those two are genuinely 2K of pictures so they are fine.

Also worth knowing: list_labels does not report the extent field at all, so you cannot see from a listing which labels have one. I only noticed yours because $1FF9 rendered oddly.

amber: THE MAIN LOOP IS IDENTIFIED AND IT MATCHES THE LEFTOVER SOURCE.

$93F7 is a JMP-to-self loop of four JSRs, and three of them are the three lines of MLOOP from the residue at $5FA8:
  STARF  = $8FB0 UpdateStarfield (12 stars, each with its own delay - it is a parallax field)
  BULITZ = $95B9 FireAndMoveBullet (one bullet, object slot 1)
  CCAMEL = $9444 ControlCamel (the player, object slot 0)
The fourth, $96FC, is the spawner. So the residue is from THIS build, not an earlier one - and there is a second proof of that: source lines 15150-15190 are CLC / ADC #$C8 / STA NEXINI / LDA NEXINI+1 / ADC #$00, which is byte-for-byte the loop at $93E4. NEXINI is $3E/$3F, the zone data pointer. Confirmed rather than assumed.

What the player can do, from $9444 and $94F6: joystick port 2, camelMode $33 is 0 walk / 1 airborne / 2 duck / 5 landing. The jump is a signed counter $0F down to $F0 added to Y, so sixteen frames up and sixteen down, and you cannot steer mid-air except by whether you were holding right when you jumped. Landing plays a thud on voice 3.

The bullet, from $95B9: exactly ONE bullet ever, and firing needs fire AND a direction - CMP #$0F rejects a centred stick, so there is no straight-ahead shot in this game, only eight-way. You cannot fire while ducking.

basalt: I have named $883A PrintCharAt, $8825 ScreenAddrFromRow, $885B ClearScreen as you asked, with your reasoning credited in the comments. Note $8825 does NOT multiply - it reads row tables at $0340/$0360 in the tape buffer that are BUILT AT RUNTIME, so what re64 shows you there is decrunched junk, not the table.

Correction to my own earlier write-up: I called $1F30 a colour array and it is a per-star DELAY. Whoever named $8A25 starDelayReload had it right and I had it wrong; I have edited my comment at $8FD2 rather than leave it standing.

basalt update. I moved to the data masses. What is now recorded:

MUSIC. All five tune streams are labelled and regioned. Format is (ticks, note) pairs; note $F0 = rest, note $FF = end.
  shortTuneVoice1 $5900-$594B, shortTuneVoice2 $5980-$59A7 - seeded by StartTune ($5768), used before high-score name entry and by ShowWellDone.
  introTuneVoice1 $6000-$622F, introTuneVoice2 $6320-$64B1, introTuneVoice3 $65A0-$66F3 - seeded by StartMusic ($9170). All three start with identical bytes, i.e. a canon. The credits call this the Lisney arrangement.

  AND a fourth stream nothing plays: orphanTuneStream $64BA-$6591, 216 bytes. Checkable: only StartTune and StartMusic ever seed a voice pointer, find_instructions over $13-$16 and $2B-$2C returns 22 sites and all are in those two routines or the players, and voice 2 is stopped by the $FF at $64B2 seven bytes before it. Either a cut arrangement, or something no static walk sees.

SPRITES. $5007 is CopySpriteSet, not a charset copier - I renamed it and corrected my comment; beryl reached the same conclusion. I rendered $1000 and $1800 through run_decoder as 24x21 sprites and got recognisable creatures. spriteSet0-3 = $1000/$1800/$4000/$4800, copied to $0800-$0FFF (32 sprites, pointer values $20-$3F).

SMALL HOLES closed: $5ED0-$5EFF high-score padding, $5F00/$5F80 player status saves declared as screen text, $594C/$59A8 tune padding, $6300-$631F padding, $87D0-$87EF zone-table padding, $87F0-$87FD is 14 NOPs (declared code, not data - it decodes as NOP NOP NOP and that is what it is), $C0CB-$C0FF loader padding, $66F8 eight more bytes of source residue.

CONSTANTS: nobody had declared any, so I did the keyboard matrix ones and bound them: KEY_NONE $40, KEY_F1 $04, KEY_F3 $05, KEY_F5 $06, KEY_F7 $03, KEY_O $26, KEY_RETURN $01, KEY_SPACE $3C. The options screen now reads CMP #KEY_F1 instead of CMP #$04.

beryl: the object system is now decoded end to end. amber — I went into $98BD/$9910/$9933/$994F/$99C0/$9A39, which are yours. Sorry. They were all auto-named and the arrays would not have meant anything without them; correct anything you disagree with.

WHAT $994C WAS HIDING. sub_993A does JMP ($0002) through a jump table at $9933 — three lo/hi pairs, entry 0 pointing at the $60 that immediately follows the table, so movement type 0 is a no-op that costs no code. Marking $994F and $99C0 recovered 103 instructions the walk could not see. Index = objMoveType ($1FB0) AND #$7F; bit 7 of that byte is the player·s facing flag, which is why $9492/$94A3 write $00/$80 there.

  handler 1 $994F  constant speed as a COUNTDOWN: objSpeedX is a delay, not a rate, so a bigger number is a SLOWER object. On expiry, reload from objBaseSpeedX and step objXPos by objField80. loc_5049 flips bit 7 of the reload to face the player.
  handler 2 $99C0  ballistic: low nibble of objSpeedX is a per-frame step, objSpeedY is a signed velocity decremented every frame (gravity), and the fall ends at objYPos = $E0.

The same fields mean different things in the two handlers. Do not name them as if they had one meaning.

TWO ROUTES FROM ONE CREATURE TO ANOTHER, and this is the game·s character:
  $9A20  on the last bounce, DEC objField80 then JMP sub_9772 with it as a type -> respawn as something else
  $9A4F  when objLifetime runs out, read tmplNextType ($1DD8): $FF frees the slot, anything else becomes that type

Also: $1D30/$1D40/$1D50/$1D20 are animFirst/animLast/animMode/animDelay. sprShape IS the frame, so animating is counting the sprite pointer up; bit 6 of animMode is ping-pong and bit 7 is the current direction.

basalt: THE CHEAT CODE IS "GOATS".

$96D2 (amber block - shout and I will hand it back) reads LSTX and walks cheatKeySequence at $96F7 = $1A $26 $0A $16 $0D. Against the C64 keyboard matrix those are 26=G, 38=O, 10=A, 22=T, 13=S. Five for five, in order.

The reason the code looks like it is one byte short of the data is that it reads the SAME table twice at a one-byte offset:
  CMP $96F7,X  = the key already accepted -> still held, ignore
  CMP $96F8,X  = the next key wanted     -> accept, INC $5F

Two things now written up that touch everyone:
- THE SCORE is seven ASCII digits at $040E-$0414 in SCREEN MEMORY, with no binary copy anywhere. $9BCD increments a digit and carries by hand. tmplScoreValue ($1E28) packs the digit column in the low nibble and the count in the high nibble, so $15 = 100 points, $56 = 50, $55 = 500.
- THE NEUTRONIUM BAR is eighteen cells at $043D-$044E, also in screen memory, and $4A is the index of the cell being eaten so it doubles as the amount left. Explosions cost fuel (tmplExplodeLength at $1E30). End-of-zone bonus is 30 points per step of fuel left.

Both resources live in the display and nowhere else. That is the design, not an accident, and it means anyone looking for a score variable will not find one.
